title: A Large Family is a Polity
author: Other Feminisms
summary: Other Feminisms engages with Catherine Pakaluk's New York Times op-ed on the benefits of siblings to advance a more radical claim: that a large family is not merely a social unit but a genuine polity — a political community with its own governance, conflicts, coalitions, and norms that must be negotiated and maintained. Drawing on Pakaluk's ethnography of college-educated mothers of large families, the article extends the sibling-benefit argument: the relational complexity of a large household trains children in the actual skills of political life — navigating hierarchy, forming alliances, managing scarcity of parental attention, and developing loyalty across real difference. The author argues that contemporary culture's reduction of the family to a unit of emotional fulfillment misses the family's older function as a training ground for civic and political virtues. A large family, with its irreducible conflicts and dependencies, may do more to prepare children for democratic citizenship than any formal civic education program. The piece situates this within a broader argument about the political and social value of family forms that are currently unfashionable in educated professional culture, and asks what is lost when those forms disappear.
points: The large family as polity is more than a metaphor: the internal dynamics of a large household — hierarchy, coalition, negotiation, management of shared scarcity — are structurally identical to the dynamics of political community, and children who grow up navigating them learn political skills experientially.

Pakaluk's ethnography shows that educated mothers who chose large families consistently describe the relational complexity as a feature rather than a cost — they valued what it built in their children as much as any curriculum or enrichment activity.

Contemporary culture's reduction of family to an emotional fulfillment unit overlooks the family's older civic function: training people in commitment, negotiation across genuine difference, and responsibility to a community not of one's own choosing.

The decline of large families in educated professional culture may be producing a generation less practiced in the relational and political skills that family size historically supplied — a civic deficit that statistics on family structure do not fully capture.

The argument is substantive rather than pro-natalist in a shallow sense: the large family offers a specific developmental environment that smaller social units cannot replicate, and its disappearance represents a genuine diminishment of how political character is formed.
quotes: I enjoyed most of Catherine Pakaluk’s recent NYT op-ed “Life is Better with Siblings.” [ ] Pakaluk is the author of Hannah’s Children [ ], an ethnography of college-educated women with five or more children. She is currently working on a companion book focused on dads of large families.

Pakaluk argues that the small polity of a large family gives children more opportunities to develop character, because they must learn to live alongside unchosen people. And it means parents don’t burden themselves with the idea they must be everything to their children—they will play with, fight with, and model themselves on other people too.

These were not exceptional cases. I wasn’t even probing for them. But mother after mother described some version of the same dynamic — a struggling older child steadied, sometimes significantly, by the responsibility and tenderness of caring for a younger one.

He may follow her into a new tenderness, but it’s too early to know if it will be via a younger sibling of his own. However many kids you have, there is always a last baby, and civilizing that child requires turning outward.
